subject: ophthalmology
title: Primary glaucoma

steps.tx: Evaluation of the anterior chamber angle by **gonioscopy** is mandatory to differentiate open-angle from angle-closure glaucoma. Aqueous produced by ciliary epithelium circulates through the pupil and drains via the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm canal. In open-angle disease, gonioscopy reveals all angle structures from Schwalbe line to scleral spur and ciliary band, with outflow resistance at juxtacanalicular meshwork. Angle closure occurs when peripheral iris contacts trabecular meshwork, blocking aqueous drainage. Accurate classification determines whether therapy requires medical outflow enhancement or relief of pupillary block.
steps.say: Gonioscopy is the essential examination technique used to inspect the drainage structures within the iridocorneal angle. Normal aqueous humour is secreted by the ciliary processes, flows around the lens through the pupil, and leaves the eye through the trabecular meshwork into Schlemm canal. When inspecting an open angle, the examiner identifies Schwalbe line, the pigmented trabecular meshwork, scleral spur and ciliary body band. In angle closure, the peripheral iris touches the trabecular meshwork, obstructing drainage. Differentiating between open and closed angles guides proper management.

steps.tx: The progression of **primary open-angle glaucoma** causes insidious, painless, bilateral visual loss that patients rarely notice early. Risk factors include elevated intraocular pressure, advanced age, positive family history, myopia, thin cornea, and African descent. First-line medical therapy uses once-daily topical prostaglandin analogues to augment uveoscleral outflow, or topical beta-blockers like timolol to reduce aqueous production, avoiding the latter in asthma. Alpha-2 agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors provide add-on control. When maximum medical therapy and laser trabeculoplasty fail, trabeculectomy creates an alternative drainage fistula.
steps.say: Primary open angle glaucoma is a chronic, progressive optic neuropathy characterized by painless visual field loss that patients rarely notice early. Elevated intraocular pressure is the major modifiable risk factor, alongside advanced age, high myopia and a positive family history. First line treatment begins with topical prostaglandin analogues, which enhance uveoscleral outflow, while beta blockers decrease aqueous production but are avoided in patients with asthma. If drops and laser trabeculoplasty fail to control intraocular pressure, surgical trabeculectomy creates a new subconjunctival drainage fistula.

steps.tx: An acute attack of **primary angle closure** develops when pupillary block in a shallow anterior chamber causes the iris to occlude the trabecular meshwork. Patients experience severe periocular pain, nausea, vomiting, colored halos, and blurred vision. Examination reveals a stony hard eye, ciliary congestion, corneal edema, shallow chamber, and a vertically oval, mid-dilated, unreactive pupil. Immediate medical therapy combines intravenous mannitol, oral acetazolamide, topical beta-blockers, alpha-2 agonists, and pilocarpine. Definitive management requires bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy once corneal clarity is restored, preventing recurrence in both eyes.
steps.say: Acute angle closure glaucoma represents a severe ocular emergency caused by sudden pupillary block in an eye with a shallow anterior chamber. The iris bows forward, completely occluding the trabecular meshwork and causing an abrupt rise in intraocular pressure. Patients suffer excruciating eye pain, headache, nausea, colored halos and rapid loss of vision. The eye is red, the cornea looks cloudy, and the pupil is fixed and mid dilated. Emergency management lowers pressure with systemic acetazolamide, intravenous mannitol and topical drops, followed by bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy.

steps.tx: In **normal tension glaucoma**, characteristic optic disc excavation and visual field loss progress despite intraocular pressure remaining consistently within normal range below twenty-one millimetres of mercury. Pathogenesis involves vascular dysregulation, nocturnal hypotension, sleep apnea, Raynaud phenomenon, and migraine headaches. Disc hemorrhages and scotomas close to fixation are commoner than in high-tension glaucoma. Treatment requires lowering baseline pressure by thirty percent with topical medications or laser, while avoiding overzealous nocturnal antihypertensive treatment that compromises optic nerve head perfusion during sleep.
steps.say: Normal tension glaucoma is a subtype of open angle glaucoma where optic disc cupping and visual field loss progress despite pressure readings within normal limits. Vasospastic tendencies, Raynaud phenomenon, migraine headaches and nocturnal systemic hypotension are frequently associated with this condition. Examination often reveals flame shaped splinter haemorrhages at the disc margin and visual field scotomas close to central fixation. Management focuses on lowering intraocular pressure by thirty percent from baseline, while taking care not to lower systemic blood pressure excessively during nighttime hours.

steps.tx: Ophthalmoscopy reveals progressive **optic disc cupping**, characterized by thinning and notching of the neuroretinal rim violating the normal inferior-superior-nasal-temporal rule. As axons die, the cup-to-disc ratio enlarges, retinal vessels show bayoneting and nasal shifting at the cup margin, and splinter hemorrhages appear. Humphrey visual field perimetry maps functional loss from paracentral scotomas and nasal steps to dense arcuate scotomas and tunnel vision. Optical coherence tomography detects retinal nerve fiber layer thinning before perimetric visual field defects emerge, enabling early neuroprotective intervention.
steps.say: Glaucomatous optic neuropathy produces progressive optic disc cupping that reflects irreversible loss of retinal ganglion cell axons. Examination shows selective thinning of the neuroretinal rim, violation of the normal inferior superior nasal temporal rule, and vascular bayoneting at the cup edge. Flame shaped splinter haemorrhages at the disc border often signal active disease progression. Automated visual field testing maps corresponding functional losses, progressing from early paracentral scotomas to dense arcuate defects. Optical coherence tomography provides objective measurement of nerve fibre thinning before visual field loss appears.
